examples: This is Mr. Tanaka.
This way, please.
This is the restroom.
How do you like this product?
I'm the one who should be thanking you.
There are three of us.
fields.explain:
More polite than これ/ここ/この; suited to service, guidance and refined communication.
Gently giving directions:受付は こちら です。
Introducing someone: こちら は山田課長です。

こちら is a polite demonstrative equivalent to “この/ここ/これ” (but more polite), meaning "this side/this one/this person/our side".
For people: "this person" (polite, courteous).
For places/directions: "this way/this side".
For organizations/groups: "our side/we".
Used in directions, service, on the phone and in introductions.
fields.notes:
The phrase こちらこそ is used to reply to thanks/an apology: "the same goes for me".
On the phone/in service:こちらはABC会社でございます。 (This is ABC Company.)
“こちらになります” is a polite way of saying "this is ~" (with a service nuance).
mistakes: Confusing it with これ/ここ: to say "this is the restroom" politely, say こちらがお手洗いです (not これが…).
Using こちら for things far from the speaker → use あちら/そちら depending on distance/context.
Dropping の when modifying a noun: × こちら部屋→ correct: こちらの部屋。

rows: ここは<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>です。

fields.connection: さっき + [sentence/clause] / さっきの + N
examples: I saw Mr. Tanaka a little while ago.
Did you see the email from earlier?
I've had a headache for a while now.
It was raining until just a moment ago.
I called a little while ago.
Please send me the photo from earlier.
fields.explain:
さっき usually goes with the past: さっき行きました／来ました。
さっきから + Vている expresses a state that has continued up to the present.
さっきまで emphasizes that something has just ended.
Casual, used in conversation; in formal situations you can use 先ほど (more polite).

さっき expresses a very recent point in time in the past: "a little while ago, just now". It usually goes with the past tense, or with the progressive when used as さっきから.
さっき: a short, vague time before the present (from a few minutes to a short while).
さっきから: from a while ago until now (continuing).
さっきまで: right up until a little while ago (has just stopped).
fields.notes:
How "recent" さっき is depends on the context (usually within the last few dozen minutes).
さっき is not used for the future; for an ongoing present action, use さっきから + Vている.
In business emails, prefer 先ほど for politeness.
mistakes: Wrong tense: × さっき行きます → correct: さっき行きました。
Confusing さっき with もうすぐ (future): × さっき始まります → correct: もうすぐ始まります。
Dropping の when used as a noun modifier: × さっき店→ correct: さっきの店。

examples: Please come right now.
When I get home, I take a shower right away.
I went home right after class ended.
There is a convenience store right near the station.
As soon as I heard that story, tears came to my eyes.
fields.explain:
“すぐに” indicates a point in time or a position very close to the present reference point.
It can be placed before a verb or a time noun: すぐに行く／すぐに電話する／帰ってすぐに寝る。
In casual speech, “に” is often dropped: すぐ行くね！ → "I'll be right there!"
“すぐ” emphasizes a sense of speed with no delay; it suits situations where you want to show urgency or immediacy.

① “すぐに” expresses an action that happens right after another one, emphasizing immediacy.
② English meaning: "immediately", "right after", "at once".
③ It can express closeness in both time and space:・Time → the action happens right after.
・Space → "right near", "right next to".
“すぐに” can be used alone or combined with “あとで／前に／近くに” to emphasize the degree of closeness.
fields.notes:
“すぐに” is an adverb of time and comes before the main verb of the sentence.
It can be used in instructions and urgent directions:火事です！すぐに逃げてください！→ Fire! Get out right now!
At JLPT N5, learners only need to know the basic usage "to do something immediately".
At higher levels, “すぐに” can express a "quick emotional reaction", for example:彼はすぐに怒ります。→ He gets angry easily.
mistakes: Forgetting “に” in written language or on the JLPT:
✕ すぐ行きます → (correct in conversation, but on the JLPT write) ○ すぐに行きます。
Confusing “すぐに” with “もうすぐ”:
すぐに → immediately.
もうすぐ → soon.
“すぐに” is not used with long-lasting actions (such as 勉強しています) — only with actions that start or are brief.
JLPT N5 often asks: choose the right one of “すぐに”, “もうすぐ”, “あとで” to express the exact time.

rows: Expresses something happening right after an action
Short form of “すぐに”, used in casual conversation
Has not happened yet, but will happen in the near future
Emphasizes an action that has just happened
たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りました。

fields.connection: ぜんぜん + [negative predicate] (Vません / Aくない / Naではない)
examples: I have no money at all.
I didn't study at all yesterday.
This movie isn't interesting at all.
I didn't understand the teacher's talk at all.
Winter in Japan is cold, but winter in Vietnam isn't cold at all.
fields.explain:
Usually comes before a negative verb or negative adjective.
Emphasizes the feeling of "none at all" or "zero degree".
In conversation, "ぜんぜん + positive" can be used, as in “ぜんぜん大丈夫！” (Totally fine!) – however, this is a natural colloquial expression and is not used on the JLPT.
Suits a strong intonation or clear emotion (annoyance, surprise, emphasis).

① “ぜんぜん” is an adverb that emphasizes absolute negation: "not at all", "not in the least".
② Used together with a negative verb or negative adjective to express that an action or state does not happen at all.
③ In modern conversation, “ぜんぜん” is sometimes used with a positive meaning ("very", "totally") for emphasis — but for JLPT N5, you only need to remember the negative meaning.
fields.notes:
「ぜんぜん」 = "completely / totally / not at all" depending on the context.
In kanji it is written 「全然」, but in everyday communication it is usually written in hiragana: 「ぜんぜん」.
In modern Japanese you may hear: 「ぜんぜんOK！」, 「ぜんぜん大丈夫！」 → with the positive meaning "totally fine". However, this is colloquial and is not used in written language or on the JLPT.
mistakes: Wrongly using it with an affirmative sentence on the JLPT:
✕ ぜんぜんわかります → ○ ぜんぜんわかりません。
Confusing it with あまり: “ぜんぜん” = not at all, stronger than “あまり”.
Forgetting the negative verb: ✕ ぜんぜん勉強→ ○ ぜんぜん勉強しません。
JLPT N5 often asks: choose the right negative adverb among “あまり”, “ぜんぜん”, “ちょっと”.

rows: ぜんぜん + Vない／Adjない
ぜんぜんわかりません。
<ruby>全<rt>まった</rt></ruby>く（まったく） + Vない
Like “ぜんぜん” but used in written language or more formal situations

examples: Hello. What time is it there now?
I will visit you around 3 p.m.
Let's meet at your place tomorrow.
When is spring in your country?
It's sunny here. How about there?
Thank you for answering. Is this ABC Company?
fields.explain:
Polite: そちら is used instead of そっち/そこ to show respect to the listener.
Avoid using it directly to address a person: instead of “そちらは田中さんですか”, use “田中様でいらっしゃいますか”. However, in the context of an organization, “そちらはABC会社ですか” is natural.
Symmetrical set: こちら（our side）– そちら（your side）– あちら（a third party/far from both）.
Goes with the appropriate particle: そちらへ（toward）, そちらに（to/at）, そちらで（doing an action at that place）.

“そちら” is a polite pronoun referring to the listener's side (location, organization, group, situation on their side).
Used on the phone, in emails and in service communication to be more polite than そこ/そっち.
It can indicate a direction/destination (そちらへ), a place (そちらで) or possession (そちらのN).
In conversation, “そちらは？” is used to ask back about the listener's side (weather, situation).
fields.notes:
On the phone, you can open with: そちらはABC会社でいらっしゃいますか。
Asking about the weather/situation: そちらはどうですか／そちらの状況はいかがですか。
In service, staff often refer to themselves as こちら and to customers as そちら（のご希望） as an indirect polite form.
mistakes: Using そこ/そっち instead of そちら in formal contexts → less polite.
Wrong particle: “そちらで行きます” (incorrect) → should be “そちらへ行きます”.
Addressing the listener as そちら in every situation → can sound rude. Use the name + 様 or a suitable keigo expression.
Mixing up the demonstrative axis: こちら (our side) ≠ そちら (your side) ≠ あちら (over there).

examples: I ate breakfast. After that, I went to school.
I'll do my homework, and then watch TV.
I'll get my passport, and then go to the airport.
Please buy milk, and then buy some bread too.
Um… and also, I have a question.
fields.explain:
Clear time sequence: used to recount steps/activities of a day.
Adding something you just remembered: as a filler when listing things to buy/requests.
In plain writing and everyday conversation, それから is very common and natural.
It does not express a cause-and-result relationship; if needed, use それで／だから.

Meaning: "after that; and then; next". Used to connect actions/ideas in a clear chronological order.
Nuance: stronger in sequence than そして (neutral). Suited to listing things done one after another.
Also used like "oh, and also/by the way" when adding something you just remembered in conversation.
fields.notes:
When listing several items in instructions, まず／次に／それから／最後に create a very clear flow.
In conversation, それから can serve as a pause while the speaker thinks of what comes next, helping the rhythm sound natural.
Avoid connecting too many sentences with それから in a row; replace it with それに, そして, そのあと to avoid monotony.
mistakes: Using それから for a result relationship: incorrect. Use それで/だから.
Confusing it with そして: if you want to emphasize "chronological order", choose それから; そして just connects ideas neutrally.
Repeating それから too often in writing makes the text monotonous; mix in other connectives.

rows: <ruby>掃除<rt>そうじ</rt></ruby>した。それから<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>。

fields.connection: たいてい + V / たいてい + [sentence/clause]
examples: I usually get up at 6.
On weekends I usually watch movies at home.
Most students have part-time jobs.
This shop is usually not crowded.
Summers in Japan are usually hot.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence or before the predicate.
A general nuance, not a 100% statement.
Suited to describing habits and tendencies.

Most of the time, the majority of the time; talks about habits and general tendencies.
Stronger than “よく”, weaker than “いつも”.
Not used to mean "approximately (a number)".
fields.notes:
In advertising/news the kanji “大抵” is sometimes used.
“たいていのN” helps limit the scope of the subject: たいていの子ども, たいていの場合.
When you want to be more certain, “ほぼ/ほとんど” may be suitable, but the nuance is different.
mistakes: Using “たいてい” to estimate a number → wrong function.
Confusing it with “いつも”: its degree is stronger than “たいてい”.
Dropping “の” when used as a modifier: it must be “たいていの人”.

rows: よく<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します

fields.connection: だいたい + [quantity/N] / だいたい + V
examples: It's about 20 minutes to school.
I roughly understood the content of this book.
Lunch is about 500 yen.
The preparations are mostly finished.
A rough number is fine, so please tell me how many.
fields.explain:
Placed right before the item being estimated or at the beginning of the sentence.
Neutral, usable in almost any situation.
Suited to cases where absolute precision is not needed.

Approximates a quantity/time (about/approximately).
A general assessment, not detailed (generally/broadly).
Not used for "frequency" (unlike “たいてい”).
fields.notes:
Kanji: 大体; at N5, the kana “だいたい” is preferred.
“だいたい合っている” = roughly correct.
In conversation: “だいたいね…” introduces an idea as "generally speaking…".
mistakes: Confusing it with “たいてい” (frequency) → used in the wrong context.
Combining it with an exact number and the word “ちょうど” creates a contradiction.
Dropping “ぐらい/くらい” when you need to emphasize approximation: in many contexts “ぐらい” sounds more natural.

examples: I don't have time. So today is impossible.
It's dangerous. So please don't go near it.
I like studying. So I often go to the library.
It's raining. So I'll take an umbrella.
It's cheap. So I'll buy it.
fields.explain:
Placed after the sentence giving the reason, to lead to the conclusion.
Keep the politeness appropriate to the listener: だから → ですから.
Very natural for answering “どうして？”.

Connects a stated reason (S1) with a result/intention (S2) in the sense of "so/therefore".
Casual and direct; replace it with “ですから” when politeness is needed.
Different from “ので/から” (linking within one sentence) and “それで” (continuation of events).
fields.notes:
For an even softer tone: “ですので” (advanced) instead of “ですから”.
“だからこそ” emphasizes the positive inevitability of the result.
Avoid repeating “だから” too often in one stretch of speech.
mistakes: Omitting the reason sentence (S1) → “だから” sounds abrupt.
Confusing it with “それで” in narrative writing.
Using “だから” with superiors/customers: not polite enough → change to “ですから”.

examples: Someone is knocking on the door.
Is anyone here?
I'm looking for someone.
Could I get someone to help me?
This is someone's bag.
This weekend I'm going to see a movie with someone.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker does not know specifically who it is or does not want to say.
In questions, だれか～? suggests there may be such a person (expecting a "yes/no" answer).
In requests/calls for help, だれか～! has an urgent nuance: だれか助けて！
Polite style: どなたか (the polite form of だれか) can be used.
It is not used with the negative to mean "no one"; switch to だれも～ない.

だれか means "someone, somebody" (unspecified).
Usually used in affirmative sentences or questions to talk about a person whose identity is unknown.
Emphasizes "some person among those possible", but not "everyone" (unlike だれでも).
Goes with particles such as が, を, に, と, へ, の depending on its role in the sentence.
だれか + ません/ない is not used to mean "no one"; to say "no one", use だれも～ません/ない.
fields.notes:
As a modifier: だれかのN (example: だれかの手紙).
In conversation, the particle can be omitted if the meaning is clear: だれか来た？
Combined with もし: もし だれか困っていたら、助けましょう。 strengthens the hypothetical sense.
mistakes: Incorrect: だれか来ません。→ Correct: だれも来ません。 (no one comes)
Confusing だれか with だれでも: だれか入れます (refers to someone) ≠ だれでも入れます (anyone can enter).
Leaving out the appropriate particle: だれかに聞きます, だれかを探します, だれかと行きます.

rows: だれでも <ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できます。
Must be used with a negative
なにか / どこか / いつか
Like だれか but for things, places, time
なにか <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べます。/ どこか <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
どなたか いらっしゃいますか。

examples: Anyone can enter this library.
Anyone can understand this problem.
Anyone can take part in the event.
This is an app anyone can use.
Everyone fails sometimes.
There is a large sign so that anyone can find the entrance.
fields.explain:
Used in neutral/objective contexts (advertising, instructions, rules, introductions).
When emphasizing "no restriction on who": だれでもOK, だれでも歓迎.
Avoid using it for very personal/private things that are hard to generalize (e.g., "everyone loves this dish" may sound exaggerated).
Polite form: どなたでも for strangers/customers.

Expresses universality: "anyone can…/everyone…".
Often used in rules, announcements, and descriptions of ease or universality.
Suited to verbs of ability, right of use, degree of ease/difficulty, understanding/knowing.
Not used to say "no one" (in the negative it is easily misread as "not everyone…").
In gentle invitations/suggestions, you can use: だれでも来てください (anyone, please come).
fields.notes:
Adding は: だれでもは～ emphasizes a contrasting topic, with an emphatic nuance.
A common modifier form in advertising: だれでも簡単に～できる.
Be careful with the negative: だれでも～ない is usually understood as "not everyone…", not "no one…".
mistakes: Confusing it with だれも: "anyone/everyone" must be だれでも, not だれも.
Using だれでも + ません to say "no one" is incorrect; you must use だれも～ません.
Confusing it with みんな: みんな is "everyone" (a specific group), だれでも is "anyone" (open, conditional).

rows: だれかが <ruby>呼<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでいます。
Must be used with a negative
A specific group, does not mean "anyone"
More polite than だれでも
どなたでも <ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できます。

examples: No one came today.
No one knows about this.
I didn't talk to anyone at the party.
I'm busy, so I don't see anyone.
No one could answer that question.
It's dangerous at night, so no one goes outside.
fields.explain:
Used to negate the entire group of people who could be involved.
Adding も creates the nuance "not even one person…".
In spoken language, you can add emphasis with ぜんぜん/まったく (but be careful with the degree): ぜんぜん だれも来ない。
In the past tense: だれも来ませんでした keeps the meaning "no one…(did)".

だれも～ません/ない expresses "no one …".
A form of total negation where the subject is a "person".
Combines with particles depending on the relationship: に → だれにも, と → だれとも.
Not used with the affirmative (だれも～ます/だれも～だ) in modern standard Japanese.
Emphatic when placed at the beginning of a sentence: だれも～ない → strong negation "no one at all".
fields.notes:
If you need "not even once": 一度も～ません (not once), which differs from だれも (target is people).
Do not insert が after だれも when it is the subject of a negative: usually だれも来ません (not だれもが来ません).
When politeness is needed in service: どなたも～ません/いらっしゃいません.
mistakes: Using the affirmative with だれも: Incorrect “だれも来ます” → Correct “だれも来ません”。
Forgetting to change に/と to だれにも/だれとも in the negative.
Confusing it with だれでも～ない: "not everyone…" ≠ "no one…".

rows: どこも <ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いていない。
どなたも いません。
